summary:
Penang stands under the national framework of Malaysia: the federal Penal Code 1936 offences covering "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and "gross indecency" apply in the state, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, and no Penang-specific exemption or protective statute is recorded. A visitor's exposure in Penang is set by that national framework together with the state's own Sharia enactment.

Penang is one of the Malaysian states whose Sharia enactment criminalises same-sex intimacy and cross-dressing for Muslims only, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of the cane. The enactment bars Muslim men from dressing as women; no legal definition of transgender dressing is provided. These provisions reach Muslim residents and visitors, not non-Muslims.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and the Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are reported nationally, with transgender people identified as particularly vulnerable. Penang appears in a 2022 Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters study as a place where interviewees lived, but the study documents national patterns and records no Penang-specific enforcement case.

Days after the 28 November 2025 Chow Kit sauna raid in Kuala Lumpur, police in Penang raided another sauna. No arrests, charges or outcomes from that Penang raid are recorded in this inventory.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement since the 2018 election has included an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 Johor plans for conversion-therapy centres. These are documented in other states and illustrate the national enforcement climate a visitor also enters in Penang.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees as of June 2021, and conversion therapy is openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders. The Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report of 10 August 2022 drew on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia conducted between 2018 and 2021.
localsOnly:
Malaysian citizens and Muslim residents of Penang face the state Sharia enactment's cross-dressing and same-sex provisions alongside the federal Penal Code, with no legal route to change a gender marker on identity documents. The 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex, though it was never gazetted and is not legally binding.

There are no Malaysian laws protecting LGBT people against discrimination or hate crimes, and no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law. Same-sex couples have no route to recognition. The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), defines hate speech as material that denigrates a person on grounds including sexual orientation, enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust profile is last updated 16 December 2025 and the Human Rights Watch release is dated 10 August 2022; both describe national patterns. Whether Penang's own Sharia enactment has been amended, challenged in court, or actively enforced in any specific year is unresolved in this inventory.

The outcome of the Penang sauna raid that followed the 28 November 2025 Chow Kit raid is not sourced here: arrests, charges and any resulting prosecutions remain unresolved. No Penang-specific incident of violence against a trans person, and no Penang-specific document or marker refusal, is documented in this inventory.
